clue.text: Writer who sends up letters from Port Said

indicators.note: the letters taken from the place name are to be rearranged, not read in order

explanation.surface: A satirist composes letters while staying in the Egyptian city of Port Said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letters from' looks like correspondence posted from Egypt, but it asks for the letters of PORT SAID to be rearranged. To 'send up' is to mock by imitation.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who sends up a style imitates it mockingly, which is the work of a satirical imitator.

clue.text: Appropriate financial resources of isolated group…

definitions.meaning: to appropriate is to take for oneself
the money a person can draw on
a small cut-off cluster, as of resistance

explanation.surface: Taking the funds of a cut-off community, continued in the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings in a row: to take, someone's means, and an isolated cluster. The dots lead into 2 Down.
explanation.definitionFit: To take for oneself, one's means, and a cut-off cluster are all senses of the same word.

clue.text: . and make profit, as 10 did

definitions.meaning: to yield a gain on investment
10 Across is the hero of Hardy's novel whose title says he came back home

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: making a profit, as another character did.
explanation.walkthrough: The novel referred to is Hardy's The Return of the Native, 10 Across being the native.
explanation.definitionFit: An investment that yields a gain gives a yield, and Hardy's hero comes back home in the novel's title.

clue.text: Regular letters in paper

definitions.meaning: post delivered every day
a British national newspaper

explanation.surface: Correspondence that appears regularly in a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Mail is a British national tabloid newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Post arriving every day, and the name of a British tabloid newspaper.

clue.text: Unaided as Nelson was, after Santa Cruz

definitions.meaning: without help

definitions.text: as Nelson was, after Santa Cruz
definitions.meaning: Nelson lost his right arm at Santa Cruz de Tenerife in 1797

explanation.surface: Nelson, after the attack on Santa Cruz, was on his own.
explanation.walkthrough: Admiral Nelson lost his right arm at Santa Cruz de Tenerife in 1797, leaving him with one arm.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something without help, and literally having only one arm left, as the admiral had.

clue.text: Invested thus to bring better profit, perhaps

definitions.text: Invested thus to bring better profit, perhaps

parts.words: Invested thus to bring better profit, perhaps
parts.note: a 'better' here is a gambler; money staked each way on a horse pays out if the horse finishes in the first few, and such a bet is described by this word

explanation.surface: Money put into a scheme in a particular way to yield a better return.
explanation.walkthrough: 'better' reads as the comparative of good, but it is one who bets. In racing a bet is put on, and a horse that finishes second or third has this result, paying an each-way bettor.
explanation.definitionFit: Money that is staked or invested has been put down, and a horse finishing in the frame also pays out to the punter.

clue.text: Disclose why, we hear, it's liable to sink

parts.note: to disclose secrets is to leak them

indicators.note: the word why is to be heard, giving the letter that sounds the same

parts.note: the word why sounds like the letter Y

explanation.surface: Revealing the reason a ship is likely to go down.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel letting in water is in danger of going under.

clue.text: Boxer or Pekinese, perhaps, may remove striker

definitions.meaning: a Boxer was a rebel in the Chinese uprising of 1900, and a Pekinese is a native of Peking
in cricket, a left-arm wrist-spinner's delivery of this name may dismiss the batsman on strike

explanation.surface: A dog of some breed may drive away a footballer.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxer and Pekinese look like dog breeds, but mean people from China. In cricket the striker is the batsman facing; the term is a dated, now offensive one for a left-arm wrist-spinner's delivery.
explanation.definitionFit: A dated term for a Chinese person, and also a cricket delivery that can dismiss the batsman.

clue.text: Man's cases handled by him

parts.note: Man is the Isle of Man, whose two senior judges try its legal cases

explanation.surface: A man's suitcases carried by a porter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man, which has its own judges with this title.
explanation.definitionFit: This title belongs to each of the two judges of the Isle of Man's courts.

clue.text: Kidnapped her predecessor

parts.note: Kidnapped is Robert Louis Stevenson's novel; its sequel, named after a heroine, has that novel as its predecessor

explanation.surface: A woman was abducted by the person who held her post before her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kidnapped' reads as a verb, but it is the title of Stevenson's 1886 novel; the sequel of 1893 bears a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenson's sequel to his abduction adventure is titled with the name of its Scottish heroine, so the earlier book precedes it.

clue.text: Unsettled character such as Clym Yeobright

definitions.text: Unsettled character such as Clym Yeobright

parts.words: Unsettled character such as Clym Yeobright
parts.note: Clym Yeobright is the hero of a Hardy novel about his homecoming to Egdon Heath; someone born in a place rather than having settled there

explanation.surface: Thomas Hardy's Clym Yeobright is presented as a restless, unsettled figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unsettled' suggests restlessness, but here it means not a settler: a person born in the place. Clym Yeobright is the hero of Hardy's The Return of the Native.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone born locally is indigenous rather than an incomer, and Hardy's novel title uses exactly this word for Clym.

clue.text: Play superior to Private Lives?

parts.note: Private Lives is Noel Coward's comedy; a major outranks a private, and the Shaw play here is named for a Salvation Army officer

explanation.surface: Is some play better than Coward's comedy Private Lives?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' reads as part of Coward's title, but it is the army rank; Shaw's play is named for a major.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's play is titled with an officer's rank, and a major outranks a private.

clue.text: A king enters city before dawn, perhaps

indicators.note: the A and the king go into the middle of the city name, so they are placed within it

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A monarch rides into a town in the small hours.
explanation.walkthrough: ELY is a small cathedral city in eastern England, much used in crosswords. 'perhaps' marks before dawn as just one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything happening before sunrise is at a premature hour of the day.

clue.text: Eg Tchaikovsky's overture and Orwell's novel

definitions.text: Eg Tchaikovsky's overture and Orwell's novel

parts.words: Eg Tchaikovsky's overture and Orwell's novel
parts.note: the works named are the 1812 Overture and Nineteen Eighty-Four, whose title numbers are both years divisible by four

explanation.surface: A Russian composer's overture and an English writer's novel are given as examples.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue wants the titles as numbers: 1812 and 1984 are both years with a February 29th.
explanation.definitionFit: Each title is a calendar year with an extra day added, which is the kind of year sought.

clue.text: Fish on a turbulent river — that shows style

indicators.note: turbulent water is churned up, so the letters of these words are churned into a new order

parts.note: the River Plate is the estuary between Argentina and Uruguay

explanation.surface: A fish swims on a choppy river, displaying some flair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turbulent' rearranges FISH ON A into FASHION; the River Plate (Río de la Plata) is the South American estuary.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who dresses in the latest styles and displays them is a model of elegance and modishness.

clue.text: Force to join journalists' group

definitions.meaning: to coerce someone into joining, as naval recruiters once did
a gang of reporters from the newspapers

explanation.surface: Compelling someone to join a group of reporters.
explanation.definitionFit: To coerce someone into joining, and a pack of reporters.

clue.text: Is one of the Brontes meeting a Spanish queen?

parts.note: one gives the indefinite article A
the Brontë sisters published under the pen name Bell

explanation.surface: Is one of the literary sisters being introduced to a royal from Spain?
explanation.walkthrough: The Brontës wrote as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell. Isabella of Castile was a queen of Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabella I of Castile, patron of Columbus, was a queen of Spain.

clue.text: Poet — one leaves New York in excitement

indicators.note: the letters for New York are put within what is left of the word for excitement
the letter for one goes away, departing from the word for excitement

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A poet departs for New York amid great excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excitement' is TENSION; 'one leaves' drops its I, and 'in' then sets the state abbreviation into what remains, between TEN and SON.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, Lord Tennyson was a Victorian Poet Laureate.

clue.text: Giving workers breaks in word games

definitions.meaning: to spell someone is to relieve them for a spell; the hive's workers are insects, so relieving those insects
contests in which competitors must correctly say the letters of words

explanation.surface: Granting staff rest periods during games of words.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half reads literally as relieving hive insects: to 'spell' a worker is to take over so they can rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Relieving the hive's workers is a pun on the competitions where children must say how words are written.

clue.text: Wicked Svengali or poor Trilby

definitions.meaning: Svengali, the sinister hypnotist in du Maurier's novel Trilby, is a rogue
a trilby is a soft felt hat, so a shabby one

explanation.surface: In du Maurier's novel the wicked hypnotist Svengali preys on poor Trilby.
explanation.walkthrough: Both names come from George du Maurier's novel Trilby; a trilby is also a soft felt hat named after the book.
explanation.definitionFit: A villain is a rogue in British slang, and a shabby piece of headwear is literally that.

clue.text: Not as fat as 24?

definitions.meaning: thinner
24 Across is one who tilts, so another word for one who inclines

explanation.surface: Is someone less fat than the person in another clue?
explanation.definitionFit: Thinner in build, and also one who inclines, like the tilting surgeon of the linked clue.

clue.text: Lead borne, perhaps, in this

indicators.note: perhaps marks these letters as only one possible arrangement, inviting a reshuffle

explanation.surface: Bullets are carried in this item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges LEAD BORNE; the whole clue also defines the answer, a shoulder belt in which lead shot is carried.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier's shoulder belt holds cartridges, so lead ammunition is literally carried in it.

clue.text: Neat watch assembled in plant

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle, so one beast is an ox

explanation.surface: A tidy watch is put together in a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like tidy but is an old word for cattle; 'plant' looks like a factory but is the daisy.
explanation.definitionFit: The ox-eye daisy is a meadow flower, a type of plant.

clue.text: Room that lacks character

definitions.meaning: room as in free area or capacity
on a keyboard or in type, the blank between words carries no letter

explanation.surface: A room with no personality.
explanation.definitionFit: Room means available area, and the blank typed between words is the gap with no letter or symbol in it.

clue.text: Was he inclined to be a surgeon?

definitions.text: Was he inclined to be a surgeon?

parts.words: Was he inclined to be a surgeon?
parts.note: a ship that leans to one side is said to list, so one who lists is inclined; it is also the surname of the Victorian pioneer of antiseptic surgery

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone felt drawn to a medical career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inclined' means leaning, not willing: to list is to tilt. Joseph Lister pioneered antiseptic surgery.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph, the antiseptic pioneer, bore a surname that also means one who tilts to one side.

clue.text: Battle with mountainous onlookers

definitions.meaning: the Greek victory over Persia in 490 BC
Byron wrote that 'the mountains look on' this Greek plain, so peaks are its spectators

explanation.surface: A fight watched by huge crowds of spectators.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half alludes to Byron's lines in Don Juan: 'The mountains look on Marathon — and Marathon looks on the sea'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek plain was the site of a famous clash, and Byron's poem pictures mountains gazing down on it.

clue.text: Warn he may have way round this city

indicators.note: the city is enclosed by the letters of the word way, split before and after, so the city sits inside these clue words

explanation.surface: A man may be cautioned to take a detour around the town.
explanation.walkthrough: Read in reverse: put the word WAY round this city (W before, AY after) and you get 'Warn he may'; take those letters away again to find the Dutch city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch city on the Rhine was the scene of the 1944 airborne battle.

clue.text: Take child to see changing of the guard

indicators.note: changing of the guard is a ceremony, but here the letters of the phrase are changed round

explanation.surface: Bring a youngster along to watch the ceremonial changing of the guard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing of' rearranges THE GUARD; the surface is the Buckingham Palace ceremony, a London tourist sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A female offspring is someone's child.
